response.text:
A London fog thicker than morality settles over Chancery as the interminable suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce devours lives, fortunes, and hope, and a divided narrative begins: an ironical, all-seeing voice mapping rot in high places, and the candid memoir of Esther Summerson, a modest young woman reared in secrecy and shame. Summoned with fellow wards Ada Clare and Richard Carstone by the kindly Mr. Jarndyce to Bleak House, Esther finds a home, while the wards find each other; yet Richard’s aimless charm already inclines toward Chancery’s quicksand. In fashionable circles, the dazzling Lady Dedlock swoons at a law-hand in a copied affidavit, unaccountably pierced by a past she has entombed; her lawyer, Mr. Tulkinghorn—rusty, relentless—notes the telltale tremor and begins to burrow.

Around these centers, Dickens scatters his satirical constellations: Mrs. Jellyby’s “telescopic philanthropy” neglecting her filthy home for Borrioboola-Gha; Mr. Skimpole, a childlike parasite who “never means any harm”; rag-and-bottle Krook with a feral French maid; the Smallweeds, venom in human knots; and poor Jo, the crossing-sweeper “as wot don’t know nothink.” When Nemo—a nameless law-writer and opium addict—dies in Krook’s clutter, Inspector Bucket, the new, implacable arm of the law, and Tulkinghorn move from the corpse to the Dedlocks, as Lady Dedlock’s fright upon seeing Nemo’s script suggests a forbidden bond. Esther, nursing Jo in good faith after he is hunted from curb to curb, contracts smallpox and is scarred; Mr. Guppy, a comic suitor who had once proposed out of self-interest, slinks away, while Dr. Allan Woodcourt’s quiet competence begins to matter.

Krook combusts into greasy ash in his shop—the novel’s most lurid emblem of spontaneous corruption—and the chain of papers he hoarded begins to surface: a confession in scraps that ties Esther, whose guardian-aunt was the fierce Miss Barbary, to Lady Dedlock’s youthful love for Nemo, whose real name was Captain Hawdon. Tulkinghorn corners Lady Dedlock with proof, promising public exposure; that same night he is shot dead in his chambers. Suspicion falls upon George Rouncewell, the housekeeper’s soldier-son, then upon Lady Dedlock herself, before Bucket coolly unfurls his case: the murderess is Mademoiselle Hortense, Lady Dedlock’s dismissed maid, who coveted vengeance and credulity in equal measure.

Yet exposure proceeds by other means: the last letter is found, the secret is out within the house, and Lady Dedlock, shattered and pursued by Bucket for her own safety, flees the Dedlock galleries and the spectral Ghost’s Walk into the storm. Esther tracks her mother through London’s wastes to the burial ground where Hawdon lies; too late—Lady Dedlock, still draped in her pride, is dead upon the steps. Sir Leicester, struck by apoplexy and confined, remains a monument to unyielding order, softened only by a dignified forgiveness that cannot raise the dead or untie the past.

Meanwhile Richard, who changed professions as rapidly as the wind, commits wholly to Jarndyce and Jarndyce under the vampiric solicitor Vholes, marries Ada in secret, and wastes his health in hope. When the suit at last concludes—because costs have eaten the estate to the bone—Richard collapses, dying gently in Esther’s arms as Ada reveals she is with child. Mr. Jarndyce, who once asked Esther to be his wife, renounces his claim with exquisite generosity and gives her a new Bleak House and a future with Woodcourt, who returns from the East to practice among the poor.

Caddy Jellyby makes a bustling, affectionate marriage and learns housekeeping in spite of deportment; Miss Flite liberates her caged birds at last; Skimpole is shown up and drifts away; and Jo’s last “he wos wery good to me” haunts the conscience of any world that hunts children and worships forms. If Chancery is a machine that grinds justice into jargon, Dickens’s twin lights—Esther’s steadfast charity and Bucket’s secular competence—show a way through the fog. The book ends not with systemic salvation but with a tender circle: Esther, scarred yet loved, presiding over a modest hearth where kindness, not law, keeps the balance, and where the name “Bleak House” has become, by labor and love, the warmest irony of all.
